To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the ability of the rat hindlimb muscles to increase their blood flow during submaximal exercise is maintained in old age.
the regional BF response to Ex is profoundly altered in older rats.

the ability of the hindlimb muscles to increase blood flow in response to exercise declines with age, and that this decline is associated with an increase in blood flow to glycolytic muscles and a decrease in blood flow to oxidative muscles.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the effects of aging upon the cardiovascular response to exercise.
the mechanisms that regulate the blood flow response to exercise in the elderly.
understanding the role of muscle blood flow and its distribution to individual muscle groups in the regulation of exercise performance in the aged rat.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
aging is associated with altered regional muscle BF responses to submaximally intense Ex.
the age-related decline in the capacity for submaximal aerobic Ex is not associated with a generalized impairment of the ability of skeletal muscle to increase its BF.
aging is associated with a redistribution of muscle BF during Ex, with a decrease to highly oxidative muscles and an increase in BF to highly glycolytically active muscles.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

aging is associated with altered muscle BF and regional BF distribution during submaximal exercise, which may contribute to the age-associated decline in aerobic capacity and the inability to sustain submaximally intense exercise.
the age-related decline in submaximal Ex capacity is associated with a shift in the distribution of BF to highly glycolyic vs. highly oxidative hindlimb muscles.
the ability of older rats to redistribute blood flow to active muscle is impaired.
The main takeaway from our work is that
, in old rats, blood flow is reduced in highly oxidative muscles and increased in highly glycolytic ones during exercise.

there are significant changes in the blood flow distribution to the hindlimbs of old rats during exercise that may be related to age-related changes in muscle metabolism and/or the ability to maintain submaximal aerobic capacity.
the age-related changes in muscle blood flow are not uniform across the different muscles, but instead, are specific to individual muscles and muscle groups.
